SECTION 1

* Young people in the UK are often criticized by older generations for spending money on things like holidays or eating out, instead of saving every penny to buy a house, but the reality is that housing prices are so high and bank lending so strict that many young people will likely never be able to afford to buy a home no matter how much they save.

* The writer, a 24-year-old named Sam Webb, feels frustrated that young renters end up giving all their money to landlords who own the properties, while those same older property owners call young people irresponsible for not being able to buy their own homes.

* A second writer points out that people under 25 in the UK are legally allowed to be paid less than older workers for doing the exact same job, which makes it even harder for them to save money or get by financially.

* The so-called "national living wage" in the UK does not apply to workers under 25, meaning younger workers can earn significantly less per hour — as low as £7.05 for ages 21-24 and £5.60 for ages 18-20 — resulting in very low annual earnings even when working full-time.

* On top of lower wages, young people are also more likely to be employed on zero-hours contracts, which means they have no guaranteed working hours and therefore no guaranteed income, making their financial situation even more unstable and uncertain.
